title.source: Checking a claim before you share it

essentialQuestion.source: How can you find out if a story is true before you share it?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you know whether a story is true before you share it?

learningGoal.source: Use lateral reading to check a made-up news story against other sources, explain why copies add no evidence, and decide whether to share it.
learningGoal.back: Use lateral reading to check a made-up news story against other sources, explain why copies add no evidence, and decide whether the story should be shared.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Ask three questions before you share

read.sections.0.text.source: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often travels fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. It said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages can spread very fast, and a shocking story often spreads fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would be closed for a whole year. The page wrote, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like this push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy for us to share something false. Before sharing, ask three questions. Who is behind this information? What is its evidence? What do other sources say? That Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence, and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations and 25 Stanford students. In one task, they compared the websites of two doctors' groups that gave advice about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were reliable. The fact-checkers quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources instead of down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time. The researchers chose a small group on purpose, so the study shows how these experts worked, not how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations, and 25 Stanford university students. In one task, they compared the websites of two doctors' associations that gave advice about bullying. Most historians thought both sites could be trusted. The fact-checkers quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This way is called lateral reading, meaning reading sideways across many sources, not reading down one page. The fact-checkers got better answers in much less time. The researchers deliberately chose a small group, so this study shows how these experts work, not how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Bullying" as "perundungan", the word Indonesian schools use; learners may know "bullying" better.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. There were 10 fact-checkers and 25 students. In one task, they looked at two doctors' groups' websites about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were good. The fact-checkers left each page fast. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster. The group was small, so the study shows how these experts worked. It does not show how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University, United States, did a study. They watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. There were 10 fact-checkers and 25 university students. In one task, they looked at the websites of two groups of doctors about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were good. The fact-checkers quickly left each page. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster. The group was small, so this study shows how these experts work. This study does not show how everyone reads.

read.sections.2.text.source: Agreement helps only when sources have their own evidence. Several websites can repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still only one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so it knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the council and say the same. The chat page only copied the first post word for word, so it adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share it; share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example with no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs take longer.
read.sections.2.text.back: Agreement between sources only helps if each source has its own evidence. Several websites can repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still only one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so the town council knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the town council and say the same thing. The chat page only copied the first post word for word, so that page adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share that post; share the town council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example because there is no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait first. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs turn out to take longer.

Share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, like with no internet. Ask a teacher, or wait. News can change. So check again later.

watch.summary.source: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way to check information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and search for what other sources say about it and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and they learn it faster. You can do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what others say about it.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way of checking information used by professional fact-checkers. Many people check a website by reading down its page. They look at how it looks and what the page says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave that page. They open new pages and look for what other sources say about that page and about who is behind it. By reading less of that page and more about it, they know more, and faster. You can do the same thing. Before trusting a page, find out who made it and what other people say about it.

educatorNotes.1.source: The research in section 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; a shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2018–19). The 45 participants, chosen on purpose rather than at random, were 10 PhD historians teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news and fact-checking organisations and 25 Stanford undergraduates. They judged live websites and searched the web on social and political issues: for example, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both reliable; most students rated the second more reliable), and who paid for a teacher-tenure lawsuit. The authors note the small samples and timed tasks. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.back: The research in section 2 is the work of Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; its shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2018–19). The 45 participants, chosen deliberately and not at random, were 10 historians with doctorates teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news organisations and fact-checking organisations, and 25 Stanford undergraduates. They judged live websites and searched the internet on social and political issues: for example, the pages of the American Academy of Pediatrics and the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both could be trusted; most students rated the second as more trustworthy), and who paid for a lawsuit about teachers' tenure. The authors note that the samples were small and the tasks timed. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.note: "Teacher-tenure lawsuit" as "gugatan hukum tentang masa jabatan tetap guru"; tenure has no exact Indonesian equivalent.

educatorNotes.2.source: Lateral reading normally needs the internet. On an offline device the activity's source cards stand in for new pages, and the print view lists them for work on paper; a teacher can also play “the other sources”. The evidence shows only the post, so learners meet the other sources in the activity. Write and Speak use what the learner found there rather than repeat the check. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
educatorNotes.2.back: Lateral reading usually needs the internet. On a device without internet, the activity's source cards stand in for new pages, and its print version lists those cards for work on paper; a teacher can also play “the other sources”. The evidence shows only the post, so learners meet the other sources in the activity. The Write and Speak steps use what the learner found there, rather than repeating the check. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
